summary: This RFC proposes a Telnet option for sending a banner from the server to the user's Telnet, to be shown on the screen independently of the application. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: A sign at the top of your screen can say important notes, such as how secret the information is, whatever program you are running.

questions: what is the output marking telnet option
how to display a banner in telnet
what is the telnet output marking option
how do telnet security banners work
subtitle: A Telnet option that lets a server send a security banner once and have the user's Telnet keep it on screen.

tldr.problem: Some military systems tie a security level to each Telnet connection and need a banner on the screen. The banner was being sent as data inside every screen of output.
tldr.mechanism: The OUTMRK option, code 27, lets the server send the banner text once in a subnegotiation, with a control flag for its position. The user's Telnet shows it and acknowledges with ACK or refuses with NAK.
tldr.outcome: The user's Telnet maintains the banner on its own and maps application output to the rest of the screen, so the server no longer needs to know the output device page size.

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 933 as a Proposed Standard, and no RFC is recorded as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Why Mark Output
sections.content:
The security architecture of some military systems identifies a security level with each Telnet connection, so a security banner must be displayed on visual display devices. The RFC cites the Department of Defense Trusted Computer System Evaluation Criteria on labeling human-readable output.

The marking was done by transmitting the banner as data within each screen. It is more efficient to send the banner once with instructions and have User-Telnet keep it up. That frees Server-Telnet from needing to know the page size of the output device.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of repainting the sign on every page, you put it up once and it stays there.

sections.title: The OUTMRK Commands
sections.content:
The option is OUTMRK, code 27. WILL, WON'T, DO and DON'T have their usual meanings about sending or receiving output marking information. Three subnegotiations carry the work:

  • IAC SB OUTMRK CNTL data IAC SE asks the receiver to use the data as a marking for normal Telnet data until further notice.
  • IAC SB OUTMRK ACK IAC SE acknowledges and agrees to use it.
  • IAC SB OUTMRK NAK IAC SE objects to using the data.

By default, with WON'T OUTMRK and DON'T OUTMRK, no marking information is exchanged.
sections.plainLanguage: The server says here is the sign, and the screen says OK or no thanks.

sections.title: How the Exchange Works
sections.content:
Either side can start, but normally the server does. The server sends WILL OUTMRK, or the user sends DO OUTMRK, and the other side accepts with the opposite. The server then sends the marking data in ASCII. User-Telnet answers with ACK (ASCII 6) or with NAK (ASCII 21). After a NAK the server must start again with more acceptable data, or take other action such as ending the connection.

After an ACK, User-Telnet must translate any cursor control commands so that application data maps to the application part of the screen. To stop marking, the server sends WON'T OUTMRK. If a WILL and DO exchange is not followed by marking data, the user side may end the option by sending DON'T OUTMRK.
sections.plainLanguage: If the screen likes the sign it says yes and shrinks the working area to fit. If not, the server must try a different sign.

sections.title: Control Flag and Banner Data
sections.content:
The CNTL flag says where the banner goes: D default (User-Telnet decides, the expected mode for most interactions), T top, B bottom, L left and R right. The precise meaning of left and right is left to be defined.

A CRLF ends a line within the banner text, and no CRLF is needed at the end. Several banners go in one subnegotiation, separated by the ASCII Group Separator (29): IAC SB OUTMRK CNTL data GS CNTL data IAC SE. User-Telnet positions the banners on the screen.
sections.plainLanguage: A letter tells the screen where to put the sign: top, bottom, left, right, or wherever it likes.
